idiom_name: bounded hand-off queue: mutex + not-empty/not-full conditions (or the runtime's channel) between producer and consumer tasks
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give the hand-off a bounded FIFO with two waiting conditions - not_empty for consumers and not_full for producers - and make insert and remove atomic under one lock, or use the runtime's channel/queue type, which packages exactly this. Insert waits while full, appends and wakes one consumer; remove waits while empty, takes the head and wakes one producer; every wait re-checks its predicate on wakeup. Choose the full-queue policy once (block, wait with timeout, reject, drop oldest/newest), design the termination protocol up front (sentinel item, close/disconnect, cancellation) so blocked waiters are released and the tail is drained, and keep items immutable or move-only across the hand-off. Scale by adding…
code_sketch:
buffer = Queue(capacity=N)            # FIFO with an explicit bound

producer:                             # once per item
    buffer.put_waiting_if_full(item)  # or try_put / timeout / drop per policy

consumer:                             # loop
    item = buffer.get_waiting_if_empty()   # or try_get / timeout
    handle(item)

# shutdown: close(buffer) or one sentinel item per consumer; release all waiters
pitfalls: Leaving the queue unbounded (or effectively unbounded) so decoupling becomes memory growth.
Writing only the happy path: no full/empty policy, no timeout and no shutdown, so blocked waiters are never released and the service cannot stop.
Handing over mutable payloads by reference while the producer keeps mutating them - the queue's synchronization is correct and the application data still races.
One queue for all work classes, coupling unrelated rates and creating head-of-line blocking.

The convoy problem: one slow consumer holding the queue lock while processing causes all other consumers (and producers via backpressure) to serialize behind it, collapsing throughput even when the queue depth is healthy.
Thread starvation: if wakeup is not distributed fairly, one consumer can monopolize the queue lock and starve others, especially under high throughput with many waiters.
Priority inversion in semaphore-based implementations: acquiring the mutex before the counting semaphore causes circular wait - always wait on the resource semaphore first, then acquire the mutex.
Using if instead of while to guard wait conditions: spurious wakeups cause the consumer to proceed on an empty buffer; always re-check the predicate in a loop.
Signaling the wrong condition variable: waking producers with not_empty or consumers with not_full wakes the wrong waiters and can cause deadlock or lost wakeups.

Not accounting for the lock convoy effect: a strict FIFO lock policy under high contention causes threads to context-switch on every lock operation once there is any queue of waiters, dramatically reducing throughput. Mitigate by keeping critical sections short, reducing lock hold time, or using a lock-free queue design.

Consumer work that blocks the event loop or executor thread: a consumer running synchronous I/O or a blocking syscall between get() and task_done() starves the loop, no getter is rescheduled, and queue depth climbs even though workers exist. Offload via executor or to_thread(), not more consumers.

Wrong move: use asyncio.Queue() with its default maxsize=0 for an unbounded burst -> memory and queueing delay grow without backpressure -> instead set a finite maxsize and choose whether put() waits, times out or sheds work.

Wrong move: let a Go pipeline stage stop reading its input while upstream keeps sending -> blocked goroutines leak and the pipeline never drains -> instead propagate cancellation through a done channel or context and close outbound channels as stages return.

Wrong move: treat Java BlockingQueue.put()/take() as a shutdown protocol -> waiters can remain blocked because BlockingQueue has no intrinsic close operation -> instead coordinate interruption or an explicit sentinel/termination protocol and drain deliberately.
